source.title: The Anatomy of Alignment: Decomposing Preference Optimization by Steering Sparse Features
source.authors: J. Ferrao; Matthijs van der Lende; Ilija Lichkovski; Clement Neo

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE features as an interpretable, largely monosemantic steering interface, but does not directly test whether individual neurons are polysemantic.
record.gate_note: The study reports activation-mass measurements for SAE style features and ablations of feature categories, which bear indirectly on feature entanglement; these are recorded under versions ["none"] because they do not measure any listed version's neuron polysemanticity claim. Benchmark results, qualitative outputs, and cited results are not rows for the claim.
record.test_reason: The study uses GemmaScope SAE features as a largely monosemantic steering basis for preference optimization. It reports its own method's behaviour: losses, ablations, benchmarks and SAE-feature activation mass. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Its use of 'polysemantic' (Appendix N) refers to SAE style-feature categories carrying about 50% of L1 activation mass, not to neuron polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with two additions. The main conclusion is that preference optimization via FSRL 'style-hacks': it relies disproportionately on style features over alignment features, and ablating style features partially restores coherence and TruthfulQA. The polysemantic-versus-auxiliary reading of the 2B and 9B style features is a secondary appendix interpretation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains an adapter to steer SAE features during preference optimization and ablates feature categories; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization or neuron-response analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report different style-feature activation mass between the 2B and 9B models and across evaluation datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Targeted style SAE features carry 45.8–52.7% of base-model L1 activation mass in Gemma-2-2B-it versus 15.8–21.2% in 9B. The authors read this as 2B style features being 'central and polysemantic'. Ablating both feature categories increases SimPO loss more than the sum of the single ablations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Gemma-2 SAE bases, the activation share and apparent entanglement of style-feature categories decrease with model scale.

record.problems: The evidence concerns SAE features and feature categories, not individual neurons or their responses to different inputs. The authors note moderate human agreement for some feature classifications (MCC 0.448–0.764), reliance on an LLM-based classifier, a limited model scale, and single-layer interventions.
record.rows_left_out: Benchmark comparisons, style-ablated benchmark outcomes, and qualitative generation examples in Sections 4–6 and Appendices M–N are not direct measurements of neuron polysemanticity. Hyperparameter sweeps, adapter-architecture comparisons, and static-steering comparisons in Appendices C and F–H concern preference optimization rather than the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No MLP neuron response measurements or layer-wise prevalence.
Superposition is assumed via SAE use, not tested.
Adapter variants change the steering policy, not the neuron polysemanticity share.

record.verdict_notes: The term 'polysemantic' is applied loosely to an LLM-classified category of SAE features, judged by activation mass. It is not a neuron-level test. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No vision models or individual vision neurons tested.
No measurement of MLP neuron responses to unrelated tokens or contexts, or their prevalence by layer.
No test of capacity pressure or whether features outnumber neurons and are packed together.
No test of polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Architectural adapter variants are compared for preference optimization, not for the share of polysemantic neurons; no SoLU, modern convnet, or neuron polysemanticity measure is tested.
No test of whether purportedly unrelated neuron responses share a feature or job.
No comparison of polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B-it
rows.operation_detail: Measured the proportion of base-model activation mass routed through the study's targeted style features.
rows.note: The authors interpret the high activation mass as indicating that targeted style features are central and polysemantic; the measure does not itself establish that a neuron responds to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Measures the share of SAE feature L1 mass in an LLM-classified style category, not neuron polysemanticity. The authors' 'polysemantic' reading is interpretation, not measurement.
